1.pericope_label: Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy, greet Philemon their beloved fellow-labourer, with Apphia, Archippus their fellow-soldier, and the church in his house, wishing them grace and peace

schools.summary: John Gill says Paul styles himself a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and not an apostle, because he was now in bonds at Rome for the sake of Christ and the Gospel, and because he was about to entreat rather than command; that Timothy is joined with him as being well known to Philemon and as adding weight to the request; and that Philemon is called dearly beloved and a fellow-labourer, which shows both the affection in which he was held and the service he rendered. Gill takes the church in his house to be a company of believers who met there for worship, and the grace and peace of the salutation to come jointly from the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. John Calvin says the singular loftiness of the mind of Paul, though it may be seen to greater advantage in his other writings which treat of weightier matters, is also attested by this Epistle, in which, while he handles a subject otherwise low and mean, he rises to God with his wonted elevation: sending back a runaway slave and thief, he supplicates pardon for him, but in pleading this cause he discourses about Christian forbearance with such ability that he appears to speak about the interests of the whole Church rather than the private affairs of a single individual. In behalf of a man of the lowest condition he demeans himself so modestly and humbly that nowhere else is the meekness of his temper painted in a more lively manner, Calvin says. In the same sense in which he elsewhere calls himself an Apostle of Christ, or a minister of Christ, he now calls himself a prisoner of Christ, Calvin says, because the chains by which he was bound on account of the gospel were the ornaments or badges of that embassy which he exercised for Christ; accordingly he mentions them for the sake of strengthening his authority, not that he was afraid of being despised, for Philemon undoubtedly had so great reverence and esteem for him that there was no need of assuming any title, but because he was about to plead the cause of a runaway slave, the principal part of which was entreaty for forgiveness. It is probable that this Philemon belonged to the order of pastors, Calvin says, for the title with which he adorns him, when he calls him fellow-labourer, is a title which he is not accustomed to bestow on a private individual. He next adds Archippus, who appears also to have been a minister of the Church, Calvin says, at least if he be the same person who is mentioned towards the conclusion of the Epistle to the Colossians, which is not at all improbable, for the designation fellow-soldier which he bestows on this latter individual belongs peculiarly to ministers. Although the condition of a soldier belongs to all Christians universally, Calvin says, yet because teachers may be regarded as standard-bearers in the warfare, they ought to be ready more than all others to fight, and Satan usually gives them greater annoyance; it is also possible that Archippus attended and shared in some contests which Paul maintained, and indeed this is the very word that Paul makes use of whenever he mentions persecutions. By employing these terms he bestows the highest praise on the family of Philemon, Calvin says; and certainly it is no small praise of a householder that he regulates his family in such a manner as to be an image of the Church, and to discharge also the duty of a pastor within the walls of his dwelling. Nor must we forget to mention that this good man had a wife of the same character, Calvin adds, for she too, not without reason, is commended by Paul.

Matthew Henry says that this epistle, though the shortest of Paul's writings and wholly taken up with a private matter, is yet full of instruction, and that the apostle's manner of address is itself a lesson: he styles himself a prisoner of Jesus Christ, not an apostle, which was a title of authority, but a title of suffering, and one fitted to move the heart of him to whom he wrote. Henry observes that Timothy is joined in the salutation, that Philemon is described by what was most amiable in him rather than by his rank, and that the mention of the church in his house shows what a blessing a godly householder may be, his family being so ordered that the assembly of the saints might meet in it. It is an honour to a house, Henry says, when it is a place where God is worshipped and where the ministers and members of Christ are welcome; and the salutation of grace and peace comprehends all that can be wished for those who are so described.

Adam Clarke says it may be thought strange that a short letter, written entirely on a private subject, without reference to the proof or defence of any doctrine of the Gospel, should by the general consent of the Church of God, from the highest Christian antiquity, have been received into the sacred canon, not only as a genuine production of St. Paul but as a piece designed by the Holy Spirit for the edification of the Church; however, such is the fact, and we may add that this very piece was held so sacred that even the ancient heretics did not attempt to impugn its authenticity or corrupt its matter, while making dangerously free with the four gospels and all the other epistles. Philemon was undoubtedly an inhabitant of Colosse and probably a Colossian by birth, Clarke says, though some suppose he was of Ephesus; it is evident from the nineteenth verse that he was converted to the Christian faith by St. Paul, and Clarke thinks it most probable that the apostle had visited Colosse before this and that the Gospel was planted there, as in all other parts of Phrygia, by himself. That Philemon was a person of some consideration in his own city and in the Church there is very evident from this epistle, Clarke says: he had a Church in his house and was so opulent as to be extensive in works of charity and in entertaining those Christians who from different quarters had occasion to visit Colosse. Whether he had any office in the Church is not clear, Clarke says: some think he was a bishop, others an elder or deacon, but of this there is no evidence, and he was probably no more than a private member, whose house, hand and property were consecrated to God, his Church and the poor. He who, by the good providence of God, has property and influence thus to employ, and a heart to do it, need not envy the state of the highest ecclesiastic in the Church of Christ, Clarke says: both the heart and the means to do secular good are possessed by few, whereas multitudes are found willing both to teach in and govern the Church. The occasion of writing this letter was that Onesimus, a slave, had on some pretence run away from his master Philemon and had come to Rome, where St. Paul was at that time in prison, though not in close confinement, for he dwelt in his own hired house, in which he assiduously preached the Gospel, being guarded only by one soldier, Clarke says; it appears that Onesimus sought out Paul, whose public preaching had rendered him famous in the city, and it is very likely that he was led to visit the apostle from having formerly seen him at his master's house in Colosse, and the word of life preached by the apostle became the means of his conversion. Being thus brought back to God he became affectionately attached to his spiritual father, Clarke says, and gave the apostle a full account of his elopement from his master, no doubt intimating his wish to return and repair the breach which he had made; and though he was now both dear and necessary to St. Paul, yet, as justice required that reparation should be made, he resolved to send him back, and to remove all suspicion from the mind of Philemon he wrote this letter, in which, as Dr. Macknight expresses it, with the greatest softness of expression, warmth of affection and delicacy of address, he not only interceded for Onesimus's pardon but urged Philemon to esteem him and put confidence in him as a sincere Christian. It is generally thought that Onesimus had robbed his master, Clarke says, but there is certainly nothing in the epistle from which this can be legitimately inferred: the words about wronging or owing certainly do not prove it, for they only state a possible case, and the apostle, by appearing to assume this, greatly strengthened his own argument and met the last objection which Philemon could be supposed capable of making. There is neither justice nor piety in making things worse than they appear to be, Clarke concludes, or in drawing the most unfavourable conclusions from premises which, without constraint, will afford others more consonant to the spirit of charity. Clarke adds, following Paley, that as the letter to Philemon and that to the Colossians were written at the same time and sent by the same messenger, the same persons would be about St. Paul and join in the salutations, and accordingly we find the names of Aristarchus, Marcus, Epaphras, Luke and Demas in both epistles, while Tychicus did not salute Philemon because he accompanied the epistle to Colosse.

Albert Barnes says the apostle here designates himself not as an apostle but as a prisoner, since he was about to make a request as a favour and not to issue a command, and that the appeal of one in bonds would have peculiar force with a friend; that Timothy is associated with him as in other epistles of this period; and that Philemon is addressed as dearly beloved and a fellow-labourer, which implies that he had in some way laboured with Paul in the gospel. Barnes takes the church in the house to mean the assembly which statedly met there for worship, and observes that the salutation of grace and peace unites the customary Greek greeting with the Hebrew, and that both are asked from God the Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ jointly. Charles Ellicott says it is interesting to note the substitution of the name prisoner, appealing to sympathy, for the usual title of Apostle, embodying a claim to authority: in the other Epistles of this period the Apostle's captivity is dwelt upon mainly as a ground of glory and thankfulness and only secondarily as a cause for sympathy, whereas here, in this personal Epistle, and in accordance with St. Paul's courteous determination not to command but for love's sake to entreat, the latter aspect assumes an almost exclusive prominence. Here, as in the other Epistles, the salutation includes Timothy, as desiring to imply in him, St. Paul's own son in the faith, a closeness of connection and sympathy with the Apostle not found in others, Ellicott says; but in all cases, and especially in this, the Letter is emphatically the Letter of St. Paul alone. The name Apphia is usually taken to be the Roman name Appia, Ellicott says, but the occurrence of such a name in a Greek-Asiatic family, though of course possible, is perhaps improbable, and it has been shown that it occurs in the form Apphia in many Phrygian inscriptions and may therefore be naturally supposed to be a native name; there seems little doubt that Apphia was Philemon's wife, like himself the beloved, though not the fellow-labourer or partner of St. Paul. From the mention of Archippus we may certainly conclude that he was a member of Philemon's family, Ellicott says, the ordinary conjecture making him his son; and the name fellow-soldier, applied elsewhere only to Epaphroditus, as the name soldier of Jesus Christ is applied to Timothy, appears to denote ministerial office in Archippus, which agrees with the charge to him at the close of Colossians to take heed to his ministry and fulfil it. The specially domestic and personal character of the Epistle need not induce any limitation of the phrase about the church in the house to Philemon's own family, Ellicott says; as the joining of Timothy's name in giving the salutation did not prevent the Letter from being St. Paul's only, so the joining of the Church in the house in the receiving of the salutation does not prevent its being addressed only to Philemon and his family, who were, like himself, interested in Onesimus. A.T. Robertson says the word rendered prisoner is an old adjective from the word for a bond, apparently used here on purpose rather than apostle as more effective with Philemon, and a more touching occasion of pride as Paul writes with his manacled right hand. Timothy was with Paul in Ephesus and probably known to Philemon, Robertson says; and Philemon was a resident of Colossae and a convert of Paul's, perhaps coming to Ephesus while Paul was there and his ministry had so much influence over the province of Asia, the name occurring also in the legend of Baucis and Philemon but with no connection with the brother here. Apphia is a common name in Phrygian inscriptions and apparently the wife of Philemon, Robertson says, sister being used in the Christian sense; it is uncertain whether Archippus is the son of Philemon or not, though he is apparently prominent in the church in Colossae, possibly even pastor, and probably not in Laodicea as some understand the Colossian passage to imply. Fellow-soldier is an old word occurring only here and in Philippians in the New Testament, and is used in a metaphorical sense, Robertson says. The church in thy house means the church that met in the house of Philemon, Robertson says: in large cities there would be several meeting-places, and before the third century there is no certain evidence of special church buildings for worship; he compares Mary's house in Jerusalem, the house of Aquila and Prisca in Ephesus and again in Rome, and the house of Nympha in Laodicea.

John Chrysostom says these things are said to a master in behalf of a servant. Immediately at the outset he has pulled down his spirit, and not suffered him to be ashamed, and has quenched his anger, Chrysostom says: calling himself a prisoner, he strikes him with compunction, and makes him collect himself, and makes it appear that present things are nothing. Chrysostom takes the whole opening as calculated to dispose the hearer before anything is asked, so that the titles Paul gives himself and those he gives Philemon are alike parts of the entreaty.

debates: Why Paul calls himself a prisoner rather than an apostle: Ellicott and Robertson take it as the deliberate substitution of a title appealing to sympathy for one claiming authority, Robertson adding the image of the manacled right hand; Calvin takes it the opposite way, that the chains were the badges of his embassy and are named for the sake of strengthening his authority, though not from any fear of being despised; Chrysostom describes the effect rather than the motive, that the word pulls down the master's spirit and quenches his anger at the outset

What office, if any, Philemon held: Clarke reports the guesses that he was bishop, elder or deacon, denies there is evidence for any, and concludes he was probably a private member whose house and property were consecrated to the Church and the poor; Calvin holds the contrary, that he probably belonged to the order of pastors, since Paul does not usually call a private individual his fellow-labourer; Gill and Barnes take the title to imply only that he had in some way laboured with the apostle

Whether Onesimus was a thief as well as a runaway: Calvin calls him a runaway slave and thief without argument; Clarke denies that anything in the epistle legitimately infers a robbery, holding that the words about wronging or owing state only a possible case which the apostle assumes in order to strengthen his argument, and adding that there is neither justice nor piety in drawing the most unfavourable conclusions from premises which will bear others more consonant to charity

Whether Apphia's name is Roman or native: Ellicott says it is usually taken for the Roman Appia but thinks such a name improbable in a Greek-Asiatic family, and follows the demonstration that the form Apphia occurs in many Phrygian inscriptions; Robertson confirms that it is a common name in those inscriptions
outliers: Clarke's evidential observation that even the ancient heretics never attempted to impugn or corrupt this letter, while making dangerously free with the Gospels and all the other epistles

Clarke's reflection that a man with property, influence and a heart to use them need not envy the highest ecclesiastic, since many are willing to teach and govern the Church but few have both the means and the will to do secular good

Calvin's estimate that in pleading for one man of the lowest condition Paul seems to speak of the interests of the whole Church, and that nowhere else is the meekness of his temper painted more vividly
Robertson's observation that before the third century there is no certain evidence of special church buildings for worship, so that a large city would have several house meeting-places
Robertson's note that the name Philemon occurs in the legend of Baucis and Philemon, with no connection to the man addressed here
Calvin's remark that though every Christian is a soldier, teachers are the standard-bearers, so that Satan gives them greater annoyance
Clarke's report that Paul was not in close confinement but dwelt in his own hired house guarded by a single soldier, where Onesimus sought him out
themes: the private letter in the canon

4.pericope_label: Paul thanks God, making mention of Philemon in his prayers, hearing of his love and faith toward the Lord Jesus and toward all saints, and prays that the communication of his faith may be effectual, for the bowels of the saints are refreshed by him

schools.summary: John Gill says the apostle thanks his God, whose he was and whom he served, and makes mention of Philemon always in his prayers, which shows the constancy of his intercession for him; that the love and faith spoken of are to be distributed, faith being toward the Lord Jesus and love toward all saints, since faith cannot be exercised on saints nor love in the same way on Christ; and that the communication of his faith is the fruit and effect of it in acts of beneficence, which the apostle prays may be made effectual and evident. Gill takes the refreshing of the bowels of the saints to mean that their hearts and spirits were comforted and revived by Philemon's liberality, and observes that the apostle calls him brother, which is a title of great affection. John Calvin says it deserves attention that he at the same time prays for that very thing for which he gives thanks: even the most perfect, so long as they live in the world, never have so good ground for congratulation as not to need prayers, that God may grant to them not only to persevere till the end but likewise to make progress from day to day. This praise which he bestows on Philemon includes briefly the whole perfection of a Christian man, Calvin says: it consists of two parts, faith in Christ and love towards our neighbours, for to these all the actions and all the duties of our life relate. Faith is said to be in Christ because to him it especially looks, Calvin says, in like manner as in no other way than through him alone can God the Father be known, and in no other than in him can we find any of the blessings which faith seeks. He does not thus limit love to the saints as if there ought to be none towards others, Calvin says, for since the doctrine of love is that we should not despise our own flesh, and that we should honour the image of God which is engraven on our nature, undoubtedly it includes all mankind; but since they that are of the household of faith are united with us by a closer bond of relationship, and since God peculiarly recommends them to us, for this reason they justly hold the highest rank. The arrangement of the passage is somewhat confused, Calvin says, but there is no obscurity in the meaning, except that it is doubtful whether the adverb in the fourth verse is connected with the first clause or the second: the meaning may be that whenever the Apostle offered prayer for Philemon he interwove thanksgiving with it, because Philemon's piety afforded ground of rejoicing, for we often pray for those in whom nothing is to be found but what gives occasion for grief and tears; yet the second mode of pointing is generally preferred, and Calvin leaves his readers at full liberty to judge, though for his own part he thinks the former meaning more appropriate. In the rest of the passage there is an inversion of the natural order, Calvin says, for after having spoken of love and faith he adds, towards Christ and towards saints, while the contrast would demand that Christ should be put in the second part of the clause as the object to which our faith looks. On the communication of faith Calvin says this clause is somewhat obscure, and that it ought first to be known that the Apostle is not continuing to give the praise of Philemon but on the contrary expresses those blessings for which he prays to God, these words being connected with what he had said about making mention of him in his prayers. What blessing then did he ask for Philemon, Calvin asks: that his faith, exercising itself by good works, might be proved to be true and not unprofitable. He calls it the communication of faith because it does not remain inactive and concealed within but is manifested to men by actual effects, Calvin says: although faith has a hidden residence in the heart, yet it communicates itself to men by good works, so that it is as if he had said, that thy faith, by communicating itself, may demonstrate its efficacy in every good thing. He wishes that by its effects faith may be proved to be effectual, Calvin says, which takes place when the men with whom we converse know our godly and holy life, for everything in us that is good makes known our faith. The last phrase may be explained to mean through Christ, Calvin says, but for his own part, if he were at liberty, he would rather translate it as equivalent to in Christ, for the gifts of God dwell in us in such a manner that nevertheless we are partakers of them only so far as we are members of Christ; yet because of the words that go before he is afraid the harshness of the expression would give offence, and accordingly he has not ventured to make any alteration in the words, but only wished to mention it to his readers, that after full consideration they may choose either of those meanings which they prefer.

Adam Clarke says the words are, hearing of thy love and faith, that is, his faith in Christ Jesus and his love to the saints; several excellent manuscripts and some versions put faith before love, which makes a more natural reading, and there is no figure of speech which would vindicate our saying faith in the saints, so that if we do not allow of the arrangement in the manuscripts referred to we shall be obliged to have recourse to the transposition, because faith must refer to Jesus Christ and love to the saints. On the communication of thy faith, Clarke says the words may be understood as referring to the work of love towards the saints, the poor Christians, which his faith in Christ enabled him to perform, faith being taken here for its effects; and indeed the Greek word itself is not unfrequently used to denote liberality and almsgiving, which is very properly remarked by Theophylact here, who says that the apostle terms almsgiving the communication of faith because it is the fruit of much faith. On the words may become effectual, Clarke reports that Dr. Macknight understands them to mean that the many good offices which Philemon does to the saints may become effectual in bringing others to the acknowledgment of every good disposition which is in them towards Christ Jesus or towards his members. Instead of the word for energetic or effectual, Clarke notes, the Vulgate and some of the fathers, as well as several Latin manuscripts, have read a word meaning evident, which makes a very good sense and seems to agree best with the scope of the place; and instead of in you, the reading in us is that of all the best manuscripts, as well as of several versions and fathers.

Albert Barnes says the apostle begins, as in most of his epistles, with thanksgiving, and that he thanks God rather than praises Philemon, ascribing to grace whatever was excellent in him; that the constancy of his remembrance in prayer is a mark of the apostle's affection; and that the love and faith mentioned are to be taken distributively, faith having the Lord Jesus for its object and love the saints for theirs. Barnes takes the communication of faith to mean the making known or imparting of it by its fruits, and the prayer to be that this may be effectual in producing an acknowledgment of every good thing; and he observes that the refreshing of the hearts of the saints refers to the hospitality and relief which Philemon had shown to needy Christians. Charles Ellicott notes the almost exact verbal coincidence of the opening with the salutations in Ephesians, Philippians and Colossians, with the natural distinction that this is briefer and simpler in style. The description of a faith directed not only to the Lord Jesus but to all the saints has perplexed commentators and called out various explanations, Ellicott says. One is that faith here is simply fidelity, but this can hardly be accepted as an explanation of so well-known and almost technical a phrase as faith toward the Lord Jesus Christ. Another, noting the distinction in the original between the two prepositions here, the former signifying direction towards and the latter actual contact with its object, explains the phrase as signifying the faith which has as its object the Lord Jesus Christ but which shows itself practically towards all saints; but this, even if the word will bear the gloss, seems too artificial for such a Letter as this, Ellicott says. The comparison with the contemporaneous Letter to the Colossians, where we read of their faith in the Lord Jesus and their love toward all the saints, seems to clear up the matter, Ellicott says: we have here an equivalent phrase in which, however, by what the grammarians called chiasmus, the extremes and means correspond to each other, the idea running through the Letter being Philemon's love to the saints, and in writing of that love St. Paul cannot refrain from referring it to its true origin, the faith towards the Lord Jesus Christ, whence the broken phrase. The general idea of St. Paul's prayer for Philemon is clear, Ellicott says, that his faith may become effectual, that is, energetic and perfected, in full knowledge; this is exactly the prayer which in different forms opens all the Epistles of the Captivity, and it describes the true order of Christian life, beginning in faith, deepened by love, and so growing to knowledge. But it may be asked, why the communication of thy faith, Ellicott says: the phrase is unique, but the word rendered communication is the well-known word generally rendered communion or fellowship, except where it is used technically of the communication of almsgiving, so that the phrase should probably be rendered the communion of thy faith, that is, thy fellowship in faith. Again the question arises, with whom is this fellowship, with God or man, Ellicott asks, and the answer probably is, with both: for growth in divine knowledge the communion need only be with God, but the knowledge here is not merely of every good thing, that is, of all that is of God, but of every good thing which is in us towards Christ Jesus, so that it is the knowledge of good, that is, of God's gift, as dwelling in man by the unity which binds all to Christ Jesus. Now for knowledge of this, fellowship with man is needed as well as fellowship with God, Ellicott says: the soul which dwells alone with God, even in the holiest seclusion, knows what is good in the abstract, but not what is good in man in the concrete reality; but Philemon's house was a centre of Christian life, and St. Paul might therefore well speak of this his two-fold fellowship in faith, and pray that it might grow into full knowledge at once of God and of man as in him. That all such growth must be towards Christ Jesus, dependent on unity with him and serving to deepen such unity, is the characteristic doctrine of all this group of Epistles, Ellicott adds, especially of the Colossian Epistle, of which Onesimus was one of the bearers. The same idea is carried on in the seventh verse, Ellicott says, where St. Paul declares his special joy to have been that the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through Philemon: the word refresh is the very word used by our Lord in his gracious promise to those who travail and are heavy laden, and it is ultimately in him that the hearts of the saints are refreshed, but in this case it was through the instrumentality of Philemon, by the communion of faith to which his active love was the means of welcoming them. St. Paul uses the word not unfrequently to express the relief and rest given by Christian fellowship on earth, Ellicott says, and we find it in the Apocalypse applied to the rest with Christ in heaven. The name brother is given to Philemon here and later with a marked emphasis of affection, evidently implying some special intimacy of friendship, not apparently at Colossae but perhaps at Ephesus during St. Paul's long stay there, Ellicott says; probably Philemon, whose son Archippus is supposed to have been, was St. Paul's equal in age, and although actually his convert is not addressed as usual as his son in the faith. In this place, moreover, the title brother has a peculiar appropriateness, Ellicott concludes, for the Apostle has been speaking of the love of Philemon which made him a brother indeed to all in the family of Christ. A.T. Robertson says the word always goes with the verb of thanksgiving though far away in the Greek sentence, and that the phrase for making mention of thee occurs also in Thessalonians. Paul heard through Epaphras, and possibly from Onesimus also, Robertson says; and he spoke of thy love and thy faith towards the Lord Jesus, and by a sort of momentum, in Vincent's phrase, carries both words over to the saints, though it can be explained as chiasm also. The particle rendered that is used rather than the more common final particle, Robertson notes, and is connected with the making of mention; the fellowship of thy faith is a partnership, the genitive being objective; and the adjective rendered effectual is a common one, occurring in the New Testament only here and twice besides, the papyri using the cognate form of a mill in working order and of ploughed land. Some manuscripts read in us for in you, Robertson adds, which is a common itacism.

John Chrysostom says the apostle does not immediately at the commencement ask the favour, but having first admired the man, and having praised him for his good actions, and having shown no small proof of his love, that he always made mention of him in his prayers, and having said that many are refreshed by him, and that he is obedient and complying in all things, then he puts it last of all, by this particularly putting him to the blush. For if others obtain the things which they ask, much more Paul, Chrysostom says; if coming before others he was worthy to obtain, much more when he comes after others, and asks a thing not pertaining to himself but in behalf of another. Then, that he may not seem to have written on this account only, and that no one may say, if it were not for Onesimus thou wouldest not have written, see how he assigns other causes also of his Epistle, Chrysostom says: in the first place manifesting his love, then also desiring that a lodging may be prepared for him. Hearing of thy love, he says: this is wonderful, and much greater than if being present he had seen it, Chrysostom observes, for it is plain that from its being excessive it had become manifest and had reached even to Paul, and yet the distance between Rome and Phrygia was not small. Chrysostom infers the place from the mention of Archippus, since the Colossians were of Phrygia, and Paul directed that his letter to them should be read also in the church of the Laodiceans, Laodicea being a city of Phrygia.

debates: How faith can be said to be toward the saints: Ellicott canvasses three explanations, that faith means fidelity, that the two prepositions differ so that faith has Christ for object while showing itself towards the saints, and that the words stand in chiasmus as the Colossian parallel suggests, and prefers the last while calling the second too artificial for such a letter; Robertson describes it as momentum, Paul carrying both nouns over to the saints, while allowing chiasm; Clarke reports manuscripts and versions that place faith first and says no figure of speech would vindicate faith in the saints; Calvin grants the arrangement is confused but denies any obscurity of meaning

What the communication of faith is: Clarke takes it of almsgiving, citing Theophylact that the word is so used because liberality is the fruit of much faith, and Macknight for the effect on others; Calvin denies it is praise at all, referring it to the prayer, and takes it of faith communicating itself by good works so as to be proved effectual; Ellicott keeps the ordinary sense of fellowship and argues that the fellowship is with God and man both, since one who dwells alone with God knows what is good in the abstract but not in the concrete reality of men

Where the adverb always belongs: Calvin says it is doubtful whether it goes with the thanksgiving or with the making of mention, gives the sense either way, notes that the second pointing is generally preferred, and leaves his readers at liberty while preferring the first himself; Robertson attaches it to the verb of thanksgiving despite its distance in the sentence

What text should be read in the sixth verse: Clarke reports the Vulgate, some fathers and several Latin manuscripts reading evident for effectual, and thinks it agrees best with the scope of the place, and notes that the best manuscripts read in us for in you; Robertson mentions the same variant of us for you and explains it as a common itacism
outliers: Chrysostom's analysis of the letter's architecture, that the request is deliberately placed last, after praise and proof of love, so as to put the reader to the blush
Chrysostom's observation that Paul assigns other causes for the letter besides Onesimus, lest anyone should say that but for the slave he would not have written at all
Calvin's remark that Paul prays for the very thing he gives thanks for, since the most perfect never have such ground of congratulation as to need no prayers

Ellicott's argument that fellowship with man as well as with God is needed for the knowledge of good, because the soul alone with God knows what is good in the abstract but not what is good in man in the concrete reality
Ellicott's note that the word rendered refresh is the very word of the promise to those who travail and are heavy laden, and that the Apocalypse applies it to rest with Christ in heaven
Ellicott's inference from the address brother that Philemon was probably Paul's equal in age, since although his convert he is never called his son in the faith
Robertson's evidence from the papyri, where the word rendered effectual is used of a mill in working order and of ploughed land

8.pericope_label: Though Paul might be much bold in Christ to enjoin what is convenient, yet for love’s sake he rather beseeches, being such a one as Paul the aged, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ

schools.summary: John Gill says the apostle might be bold, that is, might use freedom and authority, in Christ, that is, by virtue of his apostolic office received from Christ, to enjoin Philemon what was fit and convenient to be done; but that he chose rather to entreat, and that for love's sake, both his own love to Philemon and Philemon's love to him and to the saints. Gill takes Paul the aged in the plain sense of an old man, worn with labours and sufferings, whose years and whose bonds together gave weight to his request; and he observes that the apostle repeats the mention of his imprisonment, since a request from one in bonds for the gospel could hardly be refused. John Calvin gives the sense of the eighth verse thus, that though he has authority so that he might justly command, yet Philemon's love makes him prefer to entreat. He claims the right to command on two grounds, Calvin says, that he is an apostle and that he is an elder; and he says that on account of Philemon's love he chooses rather to entreat, because we interpose authority in commanding those things which we wish to extort by necessity even from the unwilling, but there is no need of commanding those who willingly obey. Because they who are ready of their own accord to do their duty listen more willingly to a calm statement of what is necessary to be done than to the exercise of authority, with good reason does Paul, when he has to deal with an obedient man, use entreaty, Calvin says: by his example he shows that pastors should endeavour to draw disciples gently rather than to drag them by force, and indeed, when by condescending to entreaty he foregoes his right, this has far greater power to obtain his wish than if he issued a command. Besides, he claims nothing for himself but in Christ, that is, on account of the office which he has received from him, Calvin says, for he does not mean that they whom Christ has appointed to be apostles are destitute of authority; by adding this he means that teachers have not power to enact whatever they please, but that their authority is confined within these limits, that they must not command anything but what is proper, and in other respects consistent with every man's duty. Hence pastors are reminded that the hearts of their people must be soothed with all possible gentleness, wherever this method is likely to be more advantageous, Calvin says, but yet so as to know that they who are treated so gently have nothing less exacted from them than what they ought to do. The designation elder here denotes not age but office, Calvin concludes, and he calls himself an apostle for this reason, that the person with whom he has to deal, and with whom he talks familiarly, is a fellow-labourer in the ministry of the word.

Matthew Henry says we have here the main business of the epistle, which was to plead with Philemon on behalf of Onesimus, that he would receive him and be reconciled to him, and that many arguments are urged for this purpose. The first argument is taken from what was before noted and is carried in the illative wherefore, Henry says: seeing so much good is reported of thee and found in thee, especially thy love to all saints, now let me see it on a fresh occasion, and refresh the bowels of Onesimus and mine also in forgiving and receiving him, who is now a convert and so a saint indeed. A disposition to do good, together with past instances and expressions of it, is a good handle to take hold of for pressing to more, Henry observes. The second argument is from the authority of him that was now making this request, Henry says, for the apostles had under Christ great power in the church over the ordinary ministers as well as the members of it, for edification, and might require of them what was fit and were therein to be obeyed, which Philemon should consider; this was a matter within the compass of the apostle's power to require, though he would not in this instance act up to it. Ministers, whatever their power be in the church, are to use prudence in the exercise of it, Henry says: they may not unseasonably, nor further than is requisite, put it forth, but in all must use godly wisdom and discretion. The third argument is that, waiving the authority which yet he had to require, he chooses to entreat it of him, Henry says: it is no disparagement for those who have power to be condescending, and sometimes even to beseech, where in strictness of right they might command, and so does Paul here though an apostle, entreating where he might enjoin and arguing from love rather than authority, which doubtless must carry engaging influence with it. The fourth argument is that a circumstance of the person pleading gives additional force to his petition, Henry says, since he is such a one as Paul the aged and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ: years bespeak respect, and the motions of such in things lawful should be received with regard, while the request of an aged apostle now suffering for Christ and his gospel should be tenderly considered, for in granting it Philemon would in a manner do honour to Christ in the person of an aged suffering servant of his. The fifth argument is from the spiritual relation now between Onesimus and the apostle, Henry adds, for though of right and in a civil respect he was Philemon's servant, in a spiritual sense he was now a son to Paul, God having made him the instrument of his conversion even in prison.

Adam Clarke says it would be better to read the verse thus: wherefore, although I have much authority through Christ to command thee to do what is proper, yet, on account of my love to thee, I entreat thee. The tenderness and delicacy of this epistle, says Dr. Paley as Clarke reports him, have long been admired, and there is something certainly very melting and persuasive in this and every part of the epistle; yet the character of St. Paul prevails in it throughout, for the warm, affectionate, authoritative teacher is interceding with an absent friend for a beloved convert, and urges his suit with an earnestness befitting, perhaps, not so much the occasion as the ardour and sensibility of his own mind. Here also, as everywhere, he shows himself conscious of the weight and dignity of his mission, nor does he suffer Philemon for a moment to forget it, Clarke continues, saying, I might be much bold in Christ to enjoin thee that which is convenient; and he is careful also to recall, though obliquely, to Philemon's memory the sacred obligation under which he had laid him by bringing him to the knowledge of Christ, saying, I do not say to thee how thou owest to me even thine own self besides. Without laying aside, therefore, the apostolic character, our author softens the imperative style of his address by mixing with it every sentiment and consideration that could move the heart of his correspondent, Clarke says: aged and in prison, he is content to supplicate and entreat, and Onesimus was rendered dear to him by his conversation and his services, the child of his affliction and ministering unto him in the bonds of the Gospel, which ought to recommend him, whatever had been his fault, to Philemon's forgiveness. Everything, however, should be voluntary, Clarke says: St. Paul was determined that Philemon's compliance should flow from his own bounty, saying, without thy mind would I do nothing, that thy benefit should not be as it were of necessity but willingly, trusting nevertheless to his gratitude and attachment for the performance of all that he requested and for more. The discourse at Miletus, the speech before Agrippa, and some part or other of almost every epistle exhibit examples of a similar application to the feelings and affections of the persons addressed, Clarke observes, and it is remarkable that these pathetic effusions, drawn for the most part from the apostle's own sufferings and situation, usually precede a command, soften a rebuke, or mitigate the harshness of some disagreeable truth. On Paul the aged, Clarke says that if we allow St. Paul to have been about twenty-five years of age at the utmost in the year thirty-one, when he was assisting at the martyrdom of Stephen, then as this epistle was written about the year sixty-two he could not have been at this time more than about fifty-six years old, which could not constitute him an aged man in our sense of the term; yet when the whole length of his life is taken in, being martyred about four years after this, he may not improperly be considered an elderly man. But the word signifies not only an old man but also an ambassador, Clarke says, because old or elderly men were chosen to fulfil such an office by reason of their experience and solidity, and the same word is used in the same sense and for the same reason by the Septuagint; hence some have thought that we should translate here, Paul the ambassador, which would agree very well with the scope and even the design of the place.

Albert Barnes says that for love's sake means for the love which Philemon bears to Paul and for the common cause, and that the apostle beseeches rather than commands. On Paul the aged, Barnes says we have no means of ascertaining the exact age of Paul at this time, and that he does not recollect the apostle alluding to his age, though he often does to his infirmities, in any place except here. Doddridge supposes that at the time when Stephen was stoned, when Paul is called a young man, he was twenty-four years of age, in which case he would now have been about fifty-three, Barnes reports; while an ancient estimate makes him about thirty-five at the time of his conversion, which would have made him about sixty-three at this time. The difficulty of determining the age with any accuracy arises from the indefinite nature of the word rendered a young man in the Acts, Barnes says: that word, like the corresponding term, was applied to a man in the vigour of manhood up to the age of forty years, while Phavorinus says a man is called a young man till he is twenty-eight and an old man from forty-nine till he is fifty-six, and Varro says that a man is young till he is forty-five and aged at sixty. These periods of time, however, are very indefinite, Barnes says, but it will accord well with the usual meaning of the words to suppose that Paul was in the neighbourhood of thirty when he was converted and that he was now not far from sixty; we are to remember also that the constitution of Paul may have been much broken by his labours, his perils and his trials, so that, not advanced probably to the usual limit of human life, he may have had all the characteristics of a very aged man. The argument here is that we feel it proper, as far as we can, to grant the request of an old man, Barnes concludes, and Paul thus felt it reasonable to suppose that Philemon would not refuse to gratify the wishes of an aged servant of Christ who had spent the rigour of his life in the service of the gospel. A.T. Robertson says the participle rendered though I have is concessive, and that the phrase rendered that which is befitting is from a verb meaning to come up to requirements and so to be fitting, the idiom belonging to later writers; the apostle says he rather beseeches, that is, rather than commands, which he has a perfect right to do. On Paul the aged, Robertson says Paul is called a young man at the stoning of Stephen and was perhaps a bit under sixty now, Hippocrates calling a man aged from forty-nine to fifty-six and old after that, while the papyri use the word for an old man as in Luke of Zacharias and in Titus. But in Ephesians Paul says he is an ambassador in a chain, Robertson notes, and hence Lightfoot holds that here the word for aged stands for the word for ambassador because of common confusion by the scribes between two similar letter groups, the Septuagint using the two words interchangeably four times, with some confusion also in the papyri and the inscriptions. Ambassador is undoubtedly possible here as in Ephesians, Robertson concludes, though there is no real reason why Paul should not term himself properly Paul the aged.

debates: Whether Paul the aged means an old man or an ambassador: Clarke computes that he could be no more than about fifty-six and doubts that this makes a man aged in our sense, then reports that the word also means ambassador, since elderly men were chosen for such offices, and that the Septuagint uses the one form for the other, so that some would render it Paul the ambassador, which he thinks agrees well with the design of the place; Robertson gives the same evidence, including Lightfoot's view that the words are confused here by scribes and the fourfold interchange in the Septuagint, but concludes that ambassador is possible while there is no real reason why Paul should not call himself aged; Barnes assembles the fullest chronology and settles on an age near sixty; Calvin cuts across all of them, holding that the designation denotes not age at all but office

How old Paul was: Clarke reckons about fifty-six on the assumption that he was twenty-five at the stoning of Stephen; Barnes reports one estimate of twenty-four at the stoning, giving fifty-three, and an ancient estimate of thirty-five at his conversion, giving sixty-three, and prefers about sixty himself; Robertson says perhaps a bit under sixty; Barnes adds the qualification that a constitution broken by labours, perils and trials may give a man well short of the usual limit of life all the characteristics of great age

What the waiving of authority teaches: Calvin makes it a rule of pastoral government, that teachers may command nothing but what is proper, that they should draw gently rather than drag by force, and that foregoing a right by entreaty has far greater power than issuing a command, while adding that those so treated owe nothing less than their whole duty; Henry makes it a caution about prudence in the exercise of church power and says it is no disparagement to the powerful to beseech where they might command; Robertson simply notes that Paul had a perfect right to command

On what grounds Paul claims the right he declines: Calvin says on two, that he is an apostle and an elder, taking elder as office; Henry says the apostles had great power in the church over ministers and members alike for edification, so that the matter was within Paul's power to require though he would not act up to it; Gill takes the boldness to be freedom and authority derived from the apostolic office
outliers: The celebrated appreciation Clarke quotes, that though the tenderness of the epistle has long been admired, the character of the apostle prevails throughout, the warm and authoritative teacher interceding with an absent friend for a beloved convert

The observation, quoted by Clarke, that Paul's appeals to feeling, drawn mostly from his own sufferings and situation, usually precede a command, soften a rebuke, or mitigate the harshness of some disagreeable truth
Calvin's principle that in foregoing his right by condescending to entreaty a man has far greater power to obtain his wish than by issuing a command
Barnes's qualification that a constitution much broken by labours and perils may give a man all the characteristics of great age long before the usual limit of life
The ancient definitions Barnes collects, that Phavorinus reckoned a man young till twenty-eight and aged from forty-nine, while Varro made him young till forty-five and aged at sixty
Henry's numbering of the five arguments by which the request is urged, and his remark that a disposition to do good, with past instances of it, is a good handle for pressing to more
themes: the weight of years and chains

10.pericope_label: Paul beseeches for his son Onesimus, whom he begot in his bonds, once unprofitable but now profitable to both; he sends him back as his own heart, having wished to retain him to minister in Philemon’s stead, but would do nothing without his mind, that the benefit be willing and not of necessity

schools.summary: John Gill says the apostle now names the person for whom he entreats, calling him his son because he was the instrument of his conversion, and begotten in his bonds, which was an honour to the gospel and to the prisoner both; that Onesimus was in time past unprofitable to Philemon, being an unfaithful and a fugitive servant, but now profitable both to him and to the apostle, there being an allusion in the words to the signification of his name. Gill takes the sending of him back to be an act of justice, since the relation of servant to master was not dissolved by conversion, and the apostle's refusal to retain him without Philemon's mind to be an act of delicacy, that the kindness might be voluntary and not extorted. John Calvin says that since less weight is commonly attached to those prayers which are not founded in some cause of just commendation, Paul shows that Onesimus is so closely related to him as to afford a good reason for supplicating in his behalf; and here it is of importance to consider how deep is his condescension, when he gives the name of son to a slave, and a runaway, and a thief. When he says that Onesimus has been begotten by him, this must be understood to mean that it was done by his ministry and not by his power, Calvin says: to renew a soul of man and form it anew to the image of God is not a human work, and it is of this spiritual regeneration that he now speaks. Yet because the soul is regenerated by faith, and faith is by hearing, on that account he who administers the doctrine holds the place of a parent, Calvin says; and because the word of God preached by man is the seed of eternal life, we need not wonder that he from whose mouth we receive that seed is called a father. Yet at the same time we must believe that, while the ministry of a man is efficacious in regenerating the soul, strictly speaking God himself regenerates by the power of his Spirit, Calvin says: these modes of expression therefore do not imply any opposition between God and man, but only show what God does by means of men. When he says that he had begotten him in his bonds, this circumstance adds weight to the commendation, Calvin adds. On the sending back, Calvin says nothing could have been more powerful for assuaging the wrath of Philemon, for if he had refused to forgive his slave he would thus have used cruelty against the bowels of Paul; this is remarkable kindness displayed by Paul, that he did not hesitate to receive as it were into his bowels a contemptible slave, and thief, and runaway, so as to defend him from the indignation of his master. And indeed, if the conversion of a man to God were estimated by us at its proper value, Calvin concludes, we too would embrace in the same manner those who should give evidence that they had truly and sincerely repented.

Adam Clarke says it is evident from this verse that Onesimus was converted by St. Paul while he was prisoner at Rome, and perhaps not long before he wrote this epistle. On the words was to thee unprofitable, Clarke says the apostle is alluding to the meaning of Onesimus's name, though he uses a different Greek word to express the same idea. On whom I have sent again, Clarke lays down the principle that the Christian religion never cancels any civil relations: a slave, on being converted and becoming a free man of Christ, has no right to claim on that ground emancipation from the service of his master; justice therefore required St. Paul to send back Onesimus to his master, and conscience obliged Onesimus to agree in the propriety of the measure, but love to the servant induced the apostle to write this conciliating letter to the master. Clarke observes further that the apostle's refusal to keep Onesimus without Philemon's consent, though he had need of his service, is of a piece with the whole temper of the letter, in which nothing is to be extorted and everything left to the master's free choice.

Albert Barnes says the apostle now urges the case of Onesimus, whom he calls his son, having been the means of his conversion, and adds that he was begotten in his bonds, which gave the appeal peculiar force. Barnes notes the allusion to the meaning of the name in the words unprofitable and profitable, and that the change described is a moral one, the man who had been useless as a servant being now useful both to his master and to the apostle. On the sending back, Barnes says the apostle acted on the principle that the existing relations of society were not to be violently disturbed, and that the whole passage is so worded as to leave Philemon entirely free, the apostle declining to do anything without his mind lest the benefit should seem to be of necessity. Charles Ellicott says the words are properly, my own child whom I have begotten in my bonds, Onesimus: the name is withheld till Philemon's interest is doubly engaged, for one who is the Apostle's own child, a name of endearment given elsewhere only to Timothy and Titus, and for one who was begotten under the hardships and hindrances of imprisonment; at last the name is given, and even then comes, in the same breath, the declaration of the change in him from past uselessness to present usefulness, both to the Apostle and to his former master. Of Onesimus we know absolutely nothing except what we read here and in Colossians, Ellicott says: tradition, of course, is busy with his name, and makes him Bishop of Beroea in Macedonia, or identifies him with the Onesimus, Bishop of Ephesus, mentioned in the Ignatian Epistle to the Ephesians; the name was a common one, especially among slaves. The name Onesimus means useful or profitable, though derived from a different root from the words here used, Ellicott says, and it is hardly possible not to see in this passage a play on words, though, curiously enough, this is not noticed by the old Greek commentators; St. Paul seems to say, he belied his name in days past, he will more than deserve it now. He says to thee, for he was sending back Onesimus, and adds to me, in affectionate notice of the kindly ministrations already rendered to his spiritual father, Ellicott says. The word receive is not in the best manuscripts and is supplied here from the seventeenth verse, apparently rightly in respect of sense, to fill up a broken construction in the original, Ellicott notes; and mine own bowels means my own heart, dear to me as my own soul, for though there is a usage of the word which applies it to children as begotten of our own body, this is hardly St. Paul's usage, even though it suits very well with the phrase whom I have begotten. In the original we have a graceful distinction in two points between the two clauses of the thirteenth verse, Ellicott says: the verb in the first clause is to wish and in the second to will, while the tense in the first clause is the imperfect, I was wishing or prepared to wish, implying perhaps a suppressed condition, and in the second it is the past definite, I willed or determined finally. In the words in thy stead there is again a certain delicacy of suggestion, Ellicott says: a slave was his master's property and could act only on his master's behalf and by his consent, and St. Paul is sure that Philemon's love for him would have gladly given that consent, and so made Onesimus an instrument of willing service. The benefit derived from the service of Onesimus St. Paul acknowledges as coming from Philemon, because given with his consent, Ellicott says: he will not keep Onesimus and ask that consent by letter, lest it should be as it were of necessity, that is, lest it should wear even the semblance of constraint. A.T. Robertson says the words are a tender and affectionate reference to Onesimus as his spiritual child, the verb rendered begotten being used in the same figurative sense in the first epistle to this church, and that Paul is evidently proud of winning Onesimus to Christ though a prisoner himself. Onesimus was a common name among slaves and formed like other names of the same type, Robertson says, the word coming from a noun meaning profit and a verb meaning to profit or to help; the once to thee useless one is a pun on the meaning of the name, the adjective for useless being formed with a privative, and the phrase but now to thee and to me useful carries the play still further with a compound of the same verb, the datives being ethical. I have sent back is an epistolary aorist, Robertson says, describing the matter as it will look when Onesimus arrives; the intensive pronoun means himself, in his own person, and my very heart repeats the word used earlier in the letter, so that the apostle almost loves Onesimus as his own son.

debates: Whether the play on the name was noticed in antiquity: Ellicott says it is hardly possible not to see a play on words here, and adds that, curiously enough, the old Greek commentators do not notice it; Robertson finds the play doubled, in the adjective for useless and again in the compound for useful, and observes that the name was common among slaves; Clarke marks the allusion and notes only that a different Greek word is used to express the idea; Gill and Barnes take the allusion as plain

What the begetting of Onesimus means: Calvin insists it was done by Paul's ministry and not by his power, since to renew a soul and form it anew to the image of God is no human work, and holds that the minister is called a father only because the word he preaches is the seed of eternal life, so that no opposition between God and man is implied; Robertson simply notes the figurative use of the verb and Paul's evident pride in the conversion; Barnes and Gill take the title as marking the apostle's instrumentality

Why Onesimus is sent back: Clarke lays down that the Christian religion never cancels civil relations, so that conversion gives a slave no ground to claim emancipation, and that justice required the return while love prompted the letter; Barnes puts it as a rule that existing social relations were not to be violently disturbed; Calvin does not argue the principle but makes the appeal turn on affection, that to refuse the slave forgiveness would be cruelty against Paul's own bowels; Gill treats the return as simple justice, the relation of servant not being dissolved by conversion

How the request is kept free: Ellicott finds delicacy in the tenses, a wish in the imperfect against a settled determination in the aorist, and in the phrase in thy stead, since a slave could act only by his master's consent; he adds that Paul will not keep the man and ask consent by letter, lest the benefit wear even the semblance of constraint; Barnes says the whole is so worded as to leave Philemon entirely free
outliers: Ellicott's observation that the name of Onesimus is withheld until Philemon's interest has been doubly engaged, and is released in the same breath as the declaration of his change
Ellicott's aside that the play on the name is not noticed by the old Greek commentators
Ellicott's report that of Onesimus nothing whatever is known beyond this letter and the notice in Colossians, though tradition makes him a bishop of Beroea or of Ephesus
Calvin's remark on the depth of the condescension by which the apostle gives the name of son to a slave, a runaway and a thief
Calvin's application, that if we estimated a man's conversion at its proper value we would embrace in the same way all who give evidence of sincere repentance
Robertson's note that the sending is an epistolary aorist, describing the matter as it will appear when Onesimus arrives
Ellicott's textual observation that the word receive is absent from the best manuscripts and is supplied from a later verse to complete a broken construction

15.pericope_label: Overruled for good: parted for a season, received for ever
debates: Whether the word rendered servant proves Onesimus a slave: Barnes holds it means a servant of any kind and that nothing here shows him a slave, while Robertson says it has to be slave here and Clarke and Calvin assume it throughout
Whether for ever means lifelong service or the life eternal: Ellicott and Robertson take it absolutely, Calvin keeps the contrast on the plainer level of a lasting gain against a short loss
outliers: Ellicott's observation that the verb is passive, was parted rather than departed, so that the euphemism itself hints at a higher hand
Clarke's reading of the clause as another most delicate stroke, so that Philemon has reason to be thankful the flight happened
Barnes's inference from the mention of owing that Onesimus was in a condition to hold property or at least to be entrusted

17.pericope_label: Receive him as myself: the partner, the bond, and the debt behind it
debates: Whether the promise to repay was a genuine bond Paul could meet: Ellicott and Robertson treat it as a real note of hand and infer that Paul had money of his own, while Calvin holds that his poverty made it an indirect figure asking Philemon to cancel the account
What the title partner means: Ellicott insists on a particular bond between the two men, while Gill and Barnes take it of common faith, hope and ministry
outliers: Barnes's use of the verb rendered put to my account, which occurs elsewhere only once, to insist that reckoning never charges a man with what he has not himself done or voluntarily assumed
Clarke printing the whole of the Horace letter recommending Septimius, and pointing beyond it to Pliny's letter to Sabinianus on behalf of a servant
Chrysostom's observation that the mention of the injury is held back to the last, and that the word used is wronged rather than stolen, the offence of a friend against a friend

20.pericope_label: Joy, a lodging, and the greetings that end the letter
debates: What the letter finally asks: Calvin holds that the authority of masters is left standing and only forgiveness and restoration are sought, while Robertson reads the confidence in obedience as an expectation that Philemon will free Onesimus, and Clarke reports the same opinion in others
Whether Epaphras was a fellow prisoner in fact: Barnes thinks it probable and Clarke leaves it open, while Robertson takes the word metaphorically
outliers: Calvin's inference from the words through your prayers that what is obtained by praying is said to be given, so that prayers have no power through their own merit
Clarke's second Pliny letter, in which Sabinianus is thanked for having actually forgiven the freedman, so that the parallel case is followed to its outcome
Barnes's argument that since the gospel would ultimately destroy slavery, and Christianity annihilates nothing that is good, the system must be wrong now
